title: Chapter 122 – Eighty Percent
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

Twelve days later.

The Seal climbs one point a day, and Jian has learned to hate the number.

It sits in the corner of the register like a small cold coin: 72, 73, 74. Each dawn he goes down the Dock stair and says, "Status," and each dawn it has crept up by exactly one, never two, never a half. The crack that split it on the morning of the Purple Mansion has knit into a pale seam, like the scar on a bowl mended with gold. He can feel it when he breathes in, a faint tightness under the ribs. It does not hurt. It reminds.

He fills the days with small work. He draws from the Spring Vein every morning in the Garden, one careful point, and carries it down to bank in the Reservoir. He sleeps six hours, then seven, then eight, and Bai, who has taken to examining his tongue every third day, pronounces him a slightly less dead rat. He eats at his mother's table. He lets Pebble sit on his shoulder, where she mutters at the soup, the salt, the weather and the general carelessness of the human race.

And he does not open the door.

His father notices, because his father notices everything, and has done so since long before Jian could lie.

Wenyuan has taken to walking the Garden at dawn, in the old gray robe, with his hands behind his back and his spectacles pushed up onto his forehead. He is a Foundation Early now, three months into the step, and the Qi settles round him like a cloak he has not yet learned to wear. He does it badly. The grass bends where he walks, and the old men of the lane cross themselves as he passes. But he walks with his head up, and every dawn he stops at the herb beds where his son is kneeling and says the same thing, in the same dry voice.

"You are thinner."

"I am eating."

"You are eating like a sparrow." He lowers himself onto the garden wall, one knee at a time. "Your mother puts rice in your bowl. I watch you move it round."

"I am thinking."

"Yes. I thought so." Wenyuan does not look at him. He looks at the pale violet sky. "When I was your age I had a thought I could not put down. It was whether I had done right to bring the clan to the Orchard. Whether I had let your grandfather's quarrel eat the family. I thought about it for three years." A pause. "Your mother finally said, Wenyuan, you have been holding the same stone for so long that your hand has forgotten it is a hand. I put it down. I did not stop thinking. I only stopped carrying it."

Jian says nothing.

"I am not telling you what to do." His father rises, dusts his knees, and shuffles on. "I am telling you that a man who cannot put down a stone is not holding it any better than a man who can."

* * *

Bai finds him in the Garden on the ninth day, kneeling in the herb beds, and does not speak for some time.

The old Elder has aged since the Offering. His round face has fallen in at the cheeks, and his belly, which used to arrive a moment before him, is smaller. He stands at the end of the row with a plum in one hand and a roll of linen under his arm, and he watches Jian turn the soil as a man watches a pot he has told himself not to stir.

"Your mother," he says at last.

Jian's trowel stops.

"I did her pulse at the funeral. And again yesterday, when she brought the rice." Bai chews. "I'll tell you what I told her. I told her I'd tell you, because she asked me not to, and I've never liked being told what to do."

"Say it."

"She's sixty-one." The old man's voice is flat, the voice of a physician reading a ledger. "Qi Refining, sixth step. It's not bad for a woman who started late and nursed three children and a husband and a clan. But the sixth step buys a hundred and ten years at the outside, and she's a woman who's been underfed in the first half of her life. I'd say forty. Perhaps forty-five, if the winters are kind."

"Forty years."

"A good deal, to some people." Bai shrugs. "Your father's better off. Foundation Early since the siege. He'll see a hundred and fifty. Feng, longer. Yue, if she stays on her path, longer still. But your mother is the weak beam in the roof." He shifts the roll under his arm. "She knows. She's known for years. She's said nothing because she thought you had enough to carry."

Jian sits back on his heels. The soil is cold and damp under his knees, and the silver-thread beside him is putting up its first shy shoots, each one folded like a small green fist.

"What would it take?" he asks.

"To lift her? Foundation. Properly, by the book." Bai spits a pit into the hedge. "A Foundation Establishment pill, which you know the price of. A Nine Turn companion, which you know the price of. Four months of quiet. A steady hand to watch the nine waves." He glances sideways. "I'd do it for her myself. But I'm not the one she'd trust."

"I will."

"I know you will. I'm only telling you what it costs." The old man's eyes are very tired. "Your reservoir's down to forty-three. A Foundation pill, done right, takes a hundred. You'd have to bank for two summers to pay it, and you'd have to give up whatever else you meant to do with the points."

"Then I give it up."

"Good." Bai nods slowly. "That's the right answer. It's the wrong answer for your road, boy. But it's the right one."

He walks away down the row, small and stooped, and does not look back.

* * *

He speaks to his mother that night, in the kitchen, over the dishes.

She is washing bowls at the stone sink with her sleeves pushed to the elbow, a small gray figure in the lamplight, humming under her breath. It is the song she hummed to him as a child, the one he lost at the third tempering of his blood and then, by some mercy, found again on the road home. He stands in the doorway for a moment, listening, before he steps in.

"Mother. Bai told me."

The humming stops. Her hands go on moving in the water.

"He promised he wouldn't," she says.

"He said you asked him not to. He said he never liked being told what to do."

"That is true." A small dry sound that is almost a laugh. "I should have known."

"Why did you not tell me?"

"Because you have a great deal to carry." She sets a bowl on the rack and picks up another. "And because it is not a thing to be fixed. It is a thing to be lived with. Everyone my age is the weak beam in somebody's roof. It does not mean they should be shored up with the house's last timber."

"You are not a beam."

"I am a woman of sixty-one with a bad knee and a stall." She turns, drying her hands on her apron, and looks up at him. Her eyes are brown and tired and very clear. "I have had a good life, Jian. Better than I had any right to. I raised a clan. I saw my eldest become a man and my youngest become a woman. I was there when you came home from the mountain. If I have forty years, I will spend them well. I do not need more."

"I do."

"That is not your decision."

"It is." He keeps his voice low and level. "It is the only one I will ever make that I am sure of."

She looks at him for a long time. Then she puts down the apron, crosses the kitchen, and takes his scarred left hand in both of hers, exactly as she did in the cold garden four months ago.

"If you do this," she says, "your father goes first."

"Mother—"

"Wenyuan first. He is the one who walked in front of the clan when the rest of us were afraid. He has a hundred and fifty years if he does nothing and two hundred if he does something. I will go after." Her mouth firms. "I will not be argued with. I have been right about this family for forty years."

"And Feng? Yue?"

"Feng is a Foundation Middle. He will outlast us all." Her eyes soften. "Yue is the one who worries me. She has no root. She has a very good head and a very strange gift and nothing at all to keep her alive past ninety. I would rather you spent your points on her."

"I will spend them on all of you."

"You cannot. Not at once." She releases his hand, and her voice is gentle. "That is what it means, to be the one who holds the road. You choose, and the choosing hurts, and you do it anyway. I am sorry. I would spare you if I could."

He cannot answer. She pats his arm twice, briskly, as she did when he was seven and had skinned a knee, and goes back to the sink. After a moment, quietly, she begins to hum again.

* * *

Yue is waiting for him at the foot of the Garden stair the next morning, with a ledger under her arm and an expression he cannot read.

She is twenty-three, tall and pale, in a Sutra Hall robe the color of milk. Her black braid is pinned up like a scholar's. She does not smile. She seldom does. Pebble rides on her shoulder with her tail tucked under her chin, and the pair of them regard him with the same grave, level, slightly accusing stare.

"You have not been sleeping," says Yue.

"I am sleeping eight hours."

"Eight hours is not sleeping. It is lying down." She hands him the ledger. "I have been keeping a record. Of the door."

He opens it.

It is a school notebook, bound in gray cloth, filled with her small neat hand. Dates down the margin. Notes beside each. He reads: Day 3. Door seems warmer in the afternoon. Day 7. Pebble says the hum is lower than before. Day 9. I stood at the top of the stair at midnight and I could feel it, like a wall with a light behind it. On the facing page, in careful pencil, she has drawn a diagram of the Dock's second tier: the basin, the dome, the stair. There is a small door sketched on the far wall. There is no door on the far wall.

"Yue."

"I know." She does not look at him. "I did not go in. I only stood at the top and listened." A pause. "I have always been able to hear them. Seams. Joints. The places where one thing meets another. I thought everyone could. Pebble says only she can, and now me."

"Since when?"

"Since the door." The gray eyes lift, at last. "I did not say it was a good door. I said it was there. But Jian, I think it is looking back."

He closes the ledger.

"Then you will come with me," he says, "when I open it."

"I was going to say that." Her mouth twitches. "I was going to say it very firmly. I had a speech."

"Keep it. You may need it."

She almost laughs. It is the smallest sound, a breath through the nose, and Pebble, on her shoulder, makes a noise like a small cough of satisfaction.

* * *

Ye finds him in the Sutra Hall that afternoon, and she is not alone.

They are in the long reading room, among the lamp-stands and the low shelves, in the thin gold light that falls through the high windows. Ye is seated at the end of a table with a cup of tea she has not touched. Across from her, wrapped in a gray blanket in a deep chair, sits a very small, very old woman with a face like a map of dry rivers. Her hair is white and thin. Her hands lie in her lap like folded paper. She is looking at the floor.

"Teacher," says Ye, softly. "This is the one I told you of."

Sang Ruo lifts her head.

Her eyes are pale, and sharp, and bright with an enormous tiredness. They rest on Jian with the calm, measuring look of a woman who has spent fifty-five years reading other people's faces through a veil. "So," she says. Her voice is thin and dry as a leaf. "It is you."

"Keeper."

"Not that. Never again." The faint ghost of a smile. "I am Ruo. I am an old woman who has found her pupil. I have very little else."

She is dying. He sees it in the way the blanket lies on her thin shoulders, in the color of her lips, in the way Ye's hand moves, twice, to cover her teacher's, and withdraws. She has perhaps a season. Perhaps less. The strain of the Keeper's chair has been eating at her for half a century, and with the veil gone and the Roll abandoned, there is nothing left to hold her up.

"I have asked to see the Dock," she says.

"Teacher—"

"Hush, child. I have asked." Her eyes do not leave Jian's face. "I have never seen it. I have been told of it every day of my life. I have given it a thousand sleepers' breath. I should like, before I go, to see what I fed."

He looks at Ye. Her face is stone. Her hand has gone white on the cup.

"I will carry you down," says Jian.

"You will do nothing of the kind. I have legs." Sang Ruo straightens, a little, in the chair. "I will come when you open the door. Not before. It is the only thing I have left that is any use."

"Why then?"

"Because I knew the first Operator." The pale eyes close. "Not to speak to. Only in the Roll. I read his handwriting for thirty years, in the margins of the oldest register in the Sect. It leans backward. The t's are crossed too high." A long breath. "I have wondered for a very long time who he was writing to."

Nobody moves. The sun slants across the table. Out beyond the window, in the school courtyard, a bell begins to ring for the end of the day, and a dozen children come tumbling out into the light.

* * *

Lan Tong comes through the water on the eleventh evening, and she is early.

He is sitting in the stone chair with the lamp low, reading nothing, when the mist stirs at the foot of the Reservoir and a figure steps out of it with the slow care of a woman crossing a stream on stepping-stones. She wears the same leaf-green robe. The seven-lobed leaf at her brow is a little paler than he remembers. She lays her hands together and looks at him without speaking.

"I did not call you," he says.

"You asked a question in the night. I heard it." Lan Tong crosses the floor and sits on the lip of the basin. "You asked it three times, in your sleep. I thought it would be kinder to answer than to let you ask a fourth."

"What question?"

"What does home mean?"

He had not known he was saying it.

The Dock is silent. The lamp burns. In the corner, on a folded cloak, Pebble opens one black eye, looks at the green-robed woman, and closes it again with the air of one who has heard all this before.

"My author told me to ask you twice," says Jian slowly. "The note said, ask it twice. I do not know why."

"I do." Lan Tong folds her hands in her lap. "Ask."

He draws a breath. His voice, when it comes, is steadier than he had feared.

"Lan Tong. What does home mean?"

* * *

"It means the place you left," she says.

She says it at once, in a bright, calm, clear voice, like a woman reciting a lesson to a child. "It is the room you woke up in, in the hour before you came here. It is the city, the street, the kitchen, the people you knew. It is a real place. It is where the Gate leads. When it opens, you walk through, and you are there, in your own body, at the hour you departed. Nothing is lost. Nothing is spent. It is as though you had stepped out of a door for a moment and stepped back in."

"That is what ARK-3 tells every Operator."

"It is what I have told every Operator." The leaf at her brow trembles. "I have told it seven times. It is the answer I am bound to give. It is not false."

"But it is not the whole of it."

"No." Her dark eyes are steady. "Ask again."

He does not hesitate. His hands are quite still on his knees.

"What does home mean?"

Lan Tong looks at him for a long moment, and the mist turns slowly round the basin, and when she speaks again it is in another voice. Lower. Slower. A voice with the weight of old stone on it.

"It means the place you are kept," she says.

* * *

"The Gate does not lead back to the world you came from," says Lan Tong.

"It leads to the place where a copy of you is stored. It was made the hour before you left, when you stepped into the machine, in a bright white room, with a thin cold cap on your head. It is complete. It is perfect. It remembers everything you were that morning, down to the taste of the tea. And it has waited, in a vault, in the dark, for a very long time."

The Dock is still. Pebble's eye is open again.

"When you walk through the Gate, you are not going home. You are being restored. The body you wear is taken apart. The self you have become, Lin Jian, the knot, is unmade. The vault opens, and Ethan Cole is poured into a fresh form, and wakes in a white room, with a tag on his wrist, and no memory of a mountain." She breathes out. "That is what happened seven times. That is what the note means by the first one. The first of them wrote the instructions. The others followed."

"Followed."

"They came, they tried, they died or were opened. And each time the vault restored the original, and the original was sent again." Her voice is gentle, and it does not tremble. "I do not know why. I was not told why. It is the part of the story my author kept. I only know that he chose it."

"He chose to forget."

"Every time."

Jian shuts his eyes. He sees a corridor, bright and pale. He sees a long white room. He sees, for an instant, with a clearness that makes him gasp, a hand holding a blue plastic pen, chewed at the cap, and a sheet of lined paper on a desk.

Lin Jian does not follow, she had said. He is the name you wear on this side.

"And the sleepers?" he says, from a long way off. "The Numbers? The fire?"

"Are the cost of opening it. As the Keeper told you. All of it is true." Lan Tong's voice drops. "But I think you understand now why I said ask twice. The first answer is ARK-3's. The second answer is mine. And the difference between them is the difference between a door and a cage."

* * *

He does not move for a long time.

When he opens his eyes the lamp has burned lower, and the green-robed woman has not stirred, and Pebble, on her folded cloak, has crept out and sat down beside him with her tail curled round her feet. She does not speak. She leans, very slightly, against his boot.

"I have a question," he says, "that I am afraid to ask."

"Ask it."

"If I do not go. If I leave the Gate shut. If I seat nothing, and open nothing, and stay as I am." His mouth is dry. "What becomes of the vault?"

"It waits."

"Forever?"

"It has waited six hundred years." She tilts her head. "But I will not lie to you, Operator. A thing that waits that long begins to want. I do not mean the vault. I mean the one who built it. The first of you set a timer, and I do not know when it ends."

"How would I know?"

"You would know when the House stopped asking," says Lan Tong. "And began to take."

Somewhere above them, through a great weight of stone, a bell begins to ring in the morning. It is the Pill Hall's bell, and its note is low and dull and human, and he has never in his life been so grateful for the sound.

"Thank you," he says.

"Do not." She rises, brushing the mist from her skirts. "I have only said what I was permitted to say. There is more behind the door. It is not mine to tell."

* * *

On the twelfth morning he goes down at dawn, and the register says eighty.

He has been looking for the number for a fortnight. Now that it is here, he finds that he is afraid of it. It sits in the corner of the dome, small and plain, and beside it a second line has appeared, as quietly as the dawn.

```
OPERATOR ARK-7 :: STATUS
SEAL: 80%. THRESHOLD FOR RESTRICTED DOOR: REACHED.
CE: 17 / RESERVOIR 55.
SOUL VESSEL DOOR: COLE, ETHAN. AUTHOR: OPERATOR 1.
STATUS: AJAR (SINCE PURPLE MANSION).
OPEN? (OPERATOR LEVEL 2 CONFIRMED. CONSENT: SELF.)
WARNING: THE DOOR CANNOT BE CLOSED AFTER OPENING.

```

Do not open alone.

He reads the last line three times.

It is not a system message. It is not in the register's plain, impersonal script. It is in a different hand: the same pale letters, but leaning backward a little, with the t's crossed too high. It was written, he realizes, by the same blue plastic pen.

"Pebble," he says.

Yes.

"Fetch Yue."

Yes. She is already moving, a low gray shape crossing the floor toward the stair. At the bottom step she stops and looks back. You are very afraid.

"I am."

Good, says Pebble, with great feeling. That means you are not stupid.

She climbs, slowly, one step at a time.

Jian sits in the stone chair with his scarred hands open on his knees and the register's pale light on his face, and looks at the word at the bottom of the screen.

Alone.

It is not a warning about the Seal. He knows that. It is not a warning about the door.

It is an instruction. And it was written, in a bright white room, thirty-five years before he was born, by a man who knew exactly which of his many selves would be sitting in this chair and exactly what he would be tempted to do.

Who, he wonders, does he mean?

Above him, on the stair, the footsteps of a girl begin to descend.
